entry.title: v1.2.1090: A Russian reader can open every country course
entry.content:
v1.2.1090: A Russian reader can open every country course

Russian could read one of them. It can now read all six that are not
already written in Russian: Life in the UK, Zycie w Polsce, Vivre en
France, Vivere in Italia and Vivir en Espana join Leben in Deutschland.
That is 4731 new entries, keyed on each course's own English, Polish,
French, Italian and Spanish source text, and every one of the six is at
a hundred per cent — cards, headings and the questions that close each
lesson.

Each table draws its own line between what becomes Russian and what
stays put. An institution Russian has a name for gets that name; what a
reader will only ever meet printed on a form, a card or a doorplate
leads in the source language with one gloss beside it. So the Sejm is
the Сейм and the mairie is the мэрия, while the NHS, the codice fiscale,
the permesso di soggiorno, laicite and the Seguridad Social are left
where a reader will recognise them.

check-ru-country-translations holds all six, and it grew a rule for
exactly this: a term to protect may be written as a pair, the source
word on the left and the Russian name on the right. It bit three times
while the work was going on. Renaming the Sejm wholesale fails the
build. Three Italian cards had quietly turned the residence permit into
a Russian phrase, which would have left a reader unable to recognise the
words printed on the document. And two courses answered a quiz with the
same year in different wording, where the later spread would have
decided both with no error anywhere.

The keep comparison ignores case, because a term that opens a sentence
is capitalised in Russian too, and demanding the source casing failed
every card that began with one.

entry.title: wip: Vivir en Espana closes the set for Russian
entry.content:
wip: Vivir en Espana closes the set for Russian

The sixth and last country course, complete at 935 strings. A Russian
reader can now open any of them.

Six Spanish words stay Spanish because that is where a reader meets
them: on a card, a payslip or a counter. Four go the other way, and the
gate now holds them there — the Cortes, the autonomous community, the
town hall and the language itself all have Russian names, and the cards
about who runs the hospitals are useless if the answer is a word the
reader cannot read.

The gate caught one real collision on the way in. Two courses both
answer a question with the same year, and the two tables gave that
answer different words; the second spread would have silently replaced
the first. Both now say it the same way.

entry.title: wip: Vivre en France reads in Russian as well
entry.content:
wip: Vivre en France reads in Russian as well

The fourth country course Russian can read, complete at 1025 strings and
keyed on the French source text.

The line between what is translated and what is kept runs where Russian
itself draws it. An institution Russian has a name for gets that name;
what a reader meets printed on a doorplate or a card leads in French and
is glossed once. The mairie sits on the other side of that line, and the
gate now says so: it is the мэрия in all twenty-seven cards about it.

Laicite is the word the republic names in French because no single
Russian word carries it. It is neither atheism nor a wall between two
powers, and any one-word rendering picks one of those and is wrong.

The keep rule ignores case now. A term that opens a sentence is
capitalised in Russian too, and demanding the source casing failed every
card that began with one.

Leben in Deutschland was the only country course Russian could read.
Two more join it, both complete: 1174 strings for Life in the UK and

Both source languages go into the from list for Russian, or the picker

The gate grows two rows and one rule. A term to protect may now be

right. Twenty-nine cards talk about the Sejm, and a translation that
called it a parliament instead would read well and point the reader at
nothing. Renaming all of them fails the gate, which is how the rule was
checked.

entry.title: v1.2.1089: The Russian interface catches up, and the build stops hanging
entry.content:
v1.2.1089: The Russian interface catches up, and the build stops hanging

Fifteen strings from the two newest settings reached a Russian reader in
English, because they were added to every table but that one.

The pack-interest check also never ended. It writes through profileStorage,
which schedules a shared-storage sync, and that timer reschedules itself
every second while the request fails — as it always will with no server. The
check itself passes in under a second; only the exit was missing, so the
whole build sat behind it. Its failure path already exits; this is the other
half.

entry.title: v1.2.1088: Quick Match can be played from the number row
entry.content:
v1.2.1088: Quick Match can be played from the number row

The board was mouse-only. Every row now carries its digit, on both
sides, and a digit picks the row it is printed beside. Which column it
lands in is whichever the board is waiting for: the left with nothing
chosen, the right once the left is. So a pair is two presses, the same
rhythm as clicking. Escape puts a half-made pair back.

No modifier and no focus first. This screen has no text field, and a
board you must click into before the keys work is one nobody finds.
Typing into a field elsewhere is still left alone, as are the combos
that belong to the browser.

A digit does nothing on a row already matched or while a wrong pair is
still clearing, which is the same refusal a click gets.

The badge takes its colour from the row it sits in rather than naming
its own. It had two hardcoded greens for the matched state, which the
accent-coverage check refused: an accent the learner has changed could
never have reached them.

Played through in a browser rather than reasoned about: one to pick,
one to match, the pair landed and the count moved; escape cleared a
half-made pair; a wrong pair flashed and reset itself.

entry.title: wip: Five courses stop calling themselves German
entry.content:
wip: Five courses stop calling themselves German

The lesson kept its own shorter copy of the answer to "which language am I
teaching". That copy knew French and English and sent everything else to
German, so Polish, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Russian lessons were read
out by a German voice. direction.ts has answered this correctly for every
course all along, so the lesson asks it instead of keeping a second version
that could drift; only the English variant stays here, because a British
learner is marked against British.

Russian was missing from direction.ts too, which reached the vocabulary
screens and the practice questions as well.

Italian was absent from the name chain and so was labelled German on screen.

Naming a language there makes nine prompts reachable that carry its name.
Spanish and Portuguese had none of them in any table, so both shipped courses
have been showing those lines in English whatever language the app is in;
Polish was missing from four tables and Italian from all seven. 246 entries,
each written in the voice of its own table rather than composed from a slot.

Measured per course: de-DE, en-US, fr-FR, pl-PL, es-ES, it-IT, pt-PT, ru-RU.

entry.title: The lesson card shows what it means, and the course can be told what …
entry.content:
The lesson card shows what it means, and the course can be told what to skip

The meaning sat outside the board at a third of the size of the sentence —
the smallest thing on the card, and the one that says what any of it means.
It sits on the card now, under the target, big enough to read at a glance and
still plainly the second half. The old placement is a setting rather than a
judgement: some people deliberately do not read it. Translate withholds the
meaning in both placements, because there the meaning is the answer.

And the course had one answer for a topic somebody has no interest in: pause
the pack, which skips it entirely. That is too blunt for the ordinary case,
where you would still take the sentence if it came up and simply do not want
it before everything else. Marked packs now sort last — the same score both
Continue Learning and Listen already order by, pushed past every band it has
— while staying in the course, keeping their progress and their reviews. It
is set from the lesson list, where you are reading about a pack, or from
Profile and settings, where you decide it once about yourself.

The matching round's own ending arrived from the other direction while this
was being written, so what is added here is the gate for it: a cleared board
with nothing left to deal must stop dealing AND say so, since a board that
silently stops is indistinguishable from one still waiting to be finished.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Four cards that said something other than what they meant
entry.content:
Four cards that said something other than what they meant

A dialogue line named the document a school hands out, which every country
does differently, and the grades either side of it already said what it meant
— so it says them and stops there. The four places that genuinely teach das
Zeugnis have to name the thing, and were naming it in American; they use the
course's own English now, and the gate refuses the other word.

A gritted-road line said the trains were running patchily, which is not a
word anybody says. Now and then is, and carries the same irregular service.

The voice read the verb in things that wind me up as the weather. One
spelling, two words, and the synthesiser guesses from the sentence; the
endpoint rejects custom SSML, so the spelling sent to it is the only lever
and it now goes as wynd. Only the verb — matched by an object and a particle,
the fixed neck-in phrase, or the hyphenated noun — so wind force eight and
the wind whistles up top are untouched, along with every German Wind. Nine
verb uses in the catalogue move, six weather ones do not, and the client and
the server are held to the same list.

And the picture for to stop was the media button: a white square on a blue
tile, which reads as a road sign somebody got wrong. It is the red octagon
now, the same shape and colour in both countries, and carrying no lettering
in either language. "end" keeps the button, being an ending rather than a
halt.

entry.title: v1.2.1084: Quick Match stops dealing the same six cards over and over
entry.content:
v1.2.1084: Quick Match stops dealing the same six cards over and over

Clear the board and it dealt the identical six again, reshuffled into
new positions so it read as a new board. The footer gave it away: nought
of six matched on one side, six pairs so far on the other.

The refill advances by a whole board and wraps, which is right for a
round longer than one board. A lesson previews at most six cards and the
board holds six, so the wrap landed back on nought. With nothing else to
deal it would have looped for ever, asking for the same six pairs each
time round.

A board now refills only when there are cards it has not just shown.
With none left it stays cleared and says which it is — that these were
every phrase in the lesson, and that sentence practice is there when
you want it — rather than promising a next board that will never come.
The button to move on was already on screen.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: v1.2.1083: The note on Apfelstreusel stops saying pudding
entry.content:
v1.2.1083: The note on Apfelstreusel stops saying pudding

Pudding is a false friend and the note walked straight into it. English
pudding means dessert in general, so calling an apple crumble a hot
pudding is ordinary English — but in German Pudding is the set custard
layer, and Streuselkuchen mit Pudding is a real thing, so the sentence
read as a claim about what is inside the cake. Traditionally there is
none.

The word is gone from both halves. Apfelstreusel is described by what it
is — yeast or shortcrust base, apple, streusel on top, cold with coffee
— and the crumble by what it is: stewed apple under a crumb topping,
served hot, no base.

A native speaker caught it, in German, which is the register the note
was getting wrong.

entry.title: v1.2.1084: The Italian practice questions read in Polish too
entry.content:
v1.2.1084: The Italian practice questions read in Polish too

Vivere in Italia has had a Polish table for its lesson text and its lesson
quizzes for a while, but the practice bank had none — so the lesson was read
in Polish and then asked its 299 questions in Italian. Those questions reach a
reader in three places: folded into the stepped lesson, and through the
practice and test views that all seven country packs share.

1567 strings, keyed on the Italian of itQuestionBank.ts exactly as it stands
there, extracted from the built module and paired back by position. Another 67
of the bank's strings were already answered by the course table and are
deliberately absent.

What stays Italian follows the course table exactly, so a reader moving
between a lesson and its questions never meets one word glossed two ways:
institutions keep their Italian name, the words a person meets at a counter
keep theirs with the meaning beside them, and a place name takes its Polish
form only where Polish uses nothing else.

check-pl-bank-translation gains its fourth bank row and the Italian names to
watch: Corte costituzionale, Senato, codice fiscale, permesso di soggiorno,
INPS, INAIL.

Verified in the app, in Polish, on the daily quiz: the question, all four
options and the explanation all come back translated.
